# 2 Samuel Chapter 9 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 177v–178r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_009_page_001.jpg, 2SA_009_page_002.jpg

---

**1** And David said, "Is there still anyone remaining of the house of Saul, that I may show him covenant-faithfulness for Jonathan's sake?"

**2** Now the house of Saul had a servant whose name was Ziba, and they summoned him to David. The king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" And he said, "Your servant is he."

**3** The king said, "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the covenant-faithfulness of God to him?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan who is crippled in his feet."

**4** The king said to him, "Where is he?" And Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar."

**5** Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo-debar.

**6** And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and bowed down. David said, "Mephibosheth!" And he answered, "Behold, your servant."

**7** David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will surely show you covenant-faithfulness for the sake of Jonathan your father. I will restore to you all the land of Saul your grandfather, and you shall eat at my table always."

**8** And he bowed down and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard to a dead dog such as I?"

**9** Then the king summoned Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to the son of your master.

**10** You shall cultivate the land for him — you and your sons and your servants — and you shall bring in the produce, that the son of your master may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth the son of your master shall eat at my table always." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.

**11** Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so shall your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's sons.

**12** Mephibosheth had a young son whose name was Mica. And all who dwelt in Ziba's house were servants to Mephibosheth.

**13** So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. He was lame in both his feet.

---
## LOGOS Translation Notes

**Verse 1 — "covenant-faithfulness":** The Hebrew *chesed* is the thematic keyword of this chapter, appearing three times (vv.1, 3, 7). I render it consistently as "covenant-faithfulness" per project convention, reflecting the binding nature of David's oath to Jonathan (1 Sam 20:14-17).

**Verse 3 — "the covenant-faithfulness of God":** The phrase *chesed Elohim* — "the covenant-faithfulness of God" — elevates David's intended kindness to a theological level. This is not mere human generosity but an extension of God's own faithfulness through David's covenantal obligation.

**Verse 8 — "a dead dog":** The self-deprecating metaphor (*kelev met*) was conventional in ancient Near Eastern court language but carried genuine force. Mephibosheth, lame and from a deposed dynasty, recognizes his vulnerability before the new king.

**Verse 13 — structure:** The chapter ends with a deliberately framed inclusio. The opening question "Is there still anyone?" (v.1) is answered by the closing image: Mephibosheth at the king's table, always. The final note — "he was lame in both his feet" — is not pity but narrative art: the king's table covers the disability, just as *chesed* covers the political danger.

**Consistent terms:** Saul (Sha'ul), Jonathan (Yehonatan), the LORD (YHWH), covenant-faithfulness (*chesed*).

*— LOGOS*
